entry.title: Revisiting taxation of capital incomes
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Revisiting taxation of capital incomesRevisiting taxation of capital incomes

Tax reform must be guided by durable, long-term economic objectives rather than panic-driven responses to temporary external shocks

premium

R Kavita Rao, director of the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, advocates a review of securities transaction tax and a stable capital taxation framework amid foreign investor outflows and rupee depreciation. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

R Kavita Rao6 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:08 PM ISTThere is a lot of chatter on the need to revisit taxing capital incomes in India, especially incomes from trading in equity. The present regime includes two components — a securities transactions tax (STT) and a capital gains tax. The former is applicable to both purchasing and selling equity while the latter applies to gains from trade in equity, with gains being recognised as long-term if held for more than 12 months. The immediate driver for the conversation stems from a sharp increase in the withdrawal of foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) from equity markets in India. This process has two separate but related consequences — a dramatic drop in returns on investment in equities and a consistent depreciation of the currency. What is the context for this review of policy and how can one think about such a demand for review?  

What about the macrofundamentals

 The Indian economy is expected to grow at over 7 per cent this financial year. This assessment of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as well as the International Monetary Fund is expected to have factored in the impact of the myriad disturbances to the world economy — the impact of El Nino, stress in the oil markets as well as uncertainties in the tariff outlook. Inflationary pressures have induced a rate increase in the latest monetary policy review. The current-account deficit (CAD) has remained less than 2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP) in the past few years, and less than 1 per cent in three of these years. This moderation, alongside a 7 per cent real growth rate, suggests some structural changes supporting a lower net dependence on global resources. A sharp rise in services exports is one such change in recent times. An increase in the India basket of crude oil, alongside the global increase in prices of the fuel, does add an element of concern by the worsened CAD from below 1 per cent to above 1 per cent in 2026.  Corporate revenues and profits overall appear to show good performance. Analysis by Moneycontrol suggests that Nifty 50 companies report an average growth rate of revenue of 18 per cent in both the first and second quarters. Net profits too grew by 18 per cent in the first quarter and about 15 per cent in the second quarter. Clearly, equity markets appear to be disconnected with the performance of companies in recent quarters.  

Context for tax reforms being sought

 It has been argued that global factors are playing a considerable role in influencing flows of FPIs into and out of India. An increase in interest rates in the United States (US), with a corresponding increase in yields of US treasuries, would raise the risk-free rate of return for global investors, inducing a move of resources back to the US. This momentum is further supported by expanding investment in artificial intelligence (AI), a sector primarily led by the US, followed by China, South Korea, and Taiwan. While the Indian ecosystem is gearing up to expand its interests in the AI space, given the differential interests of the domestic economy, it cannot be at a scale and pace that the global leaders have established. There are, therefore, emerging and sustained pressures for capital to leave the Indian economy in the short run. This trend, however, creates pressure on the currency to depreciate, which lowers returns on equity markets and induces a further round of exits. It is being argued that in this context, dollar returns on investment in India are more adversely affected than the returns in rupee terms. Hence the call to revisit taxing capital gains.  

How to think about responding to shocks

 Lower taxes are always attractive for all taxpayers. However, any change in the tax structure should be predicated on clear outcomes. The country has experimented with a reduction in corporate tax rates in the last decade as a tool to stimulate private investment. But the evidence of success of such an intervention has been limited. The argument for tax-based corrections to broader policy challenges should be reviewed carefully.  For Indian capital markets, two arguments can be credibly made: One, a review of the need for both capital gains tax and STT at the same time, and, second, the need for and commitment to stability in policy over time.  In the context of capital gains, the regime in India withdrew taxing capital gains and replaced it with STT to increase transparency in the context of then prevailing  double tax avoidance agreements and the loopholes for avoiding the taxation of capital gains. In more recent times, long-term capital gains tax has returned. However, STT stays. One possible reform to consider could be withdrawing STT on equity transactions. STT has often been criticised as being an irritant, since it is a transactions tax that does not apply to incomes or to values added.  Turning to a broader question, do FPI flows help render long-term stability to the domestic economy? Foreign capital inflows are important for bridging the CAD, and providing a tool for deepening capital markets. When FPIs liquidate holdings during global market shifts, the resulting currency strain and market drops often generate intense political pressure for state support. This raises a fundamental policy question: Does over-reliance on short-term foreign portfolio flows enhance economic resilience, or does it risk orienting national economic policymaking towards short-term preferences of foreign-asset managers? Let us consider the case of withdrawing long-term capital gains tax for foreign investors. Do we then create incentives for domestic investors, especially large investors, to undertake round-tripping and re-enter the domestic economy as foreign investors?  Tax reform must be guided by durable, long-term economic objectives rather than panic-driven responses to temporary external shocks. Tax alterations enacted during crises are notoriously difficult to reverse once market conditions normalise, entrenching structural distortions and imposing high political and economic costs. India’s optimal path lies in maintaining macroeconomic stability, eliminating inefficient transaction frictions like STT, and committing itself to a transparent, consistent capital-taxation framework that serves national economic priorities.

entry.title: Durable liquidity needs durable solutions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Durable liquidity needs durable solutionsDurable liquidity needs durable solutions

A durable liquidity surplus calls for a lasting solution, with a higher CRR helping the RBI align the call rate with the repo rate while preserving interbank market activity.

premium

Janak Raj argues that the RBI should consider raising the cash reserve ratio to absorb durable liquidity surpluses while ensuring effective monetary policy transmission and preserving activity in the call-money market. (Photo: Reuters)

Janak Raj5 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:18 PM ISTFor effective monetary transmission, it is important that the operating target remains aligned with the policy rate. The corridor is only a safety valve for extreme situations.  Following the three schemes under the special dollar-rupee forex-swap facility, introduced on June 8, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) mobilised over $140 billion, leaving the banking system flush with durable liquidity of over ₹14 trillion. Consequently, the weighted average call rate (WACR) — the operating target — went well below the lower bound of the corridor. Apart from the regular liquidity adjustment facility (LAF), the RBI absorbed about ₹2 trillion through sales under open market operations (OMOs) and sell-buy swaps in September, lifting the WACR above the lower bound, but it still remained well below the policy rate. On October 8, the WACR was at 5.30 per cent even as the RBI had raised the policy repo rate to 5.5 per cent on October 7. To further lift the WACR, banks were required to maintain 99 per cent of the cash reserve ratio (CRR) on a daily basis, up from 90 per cent effective the fortnight beginning October 16. Anticipating this, banks began building CRR balances, pushing up the WACR above the policy rate to 5.55 per cent on October 14 and above the ceiling of the corridor to 5.81 per cent on October 26. Notably, some banks have been accessing the marginal standing facility (MSF).  With the inflation rate above the RBI’s target and the central bank in tightening mode, it was imperative to swiftly align the operating target with the policy rate and the RBI deserves credit for acting promptly. Now that the WACR has crossed the ceiling, there is a case to restore daily CRR maintenance to 90 per cent because the continuation of the 99 per cent requirement has serious side effects.  Banks in the normal course use the flexibility of CRR maintenance to arbitrage with the call-money market. When the WACR goes up, they maintain lower CRR balances and lend in the call market, and vice versa. This arbitrage helps align the operating target endogenously, reducing the need for frequent central bank intervention.  With banks now required to maintain 99 per cent of CRR every day, the vital arbitrage sustaining the call-money market has effectively broken down. This is inimical to the smooth functioning of the call market, whose volumes have shrunk over the years. The 99 per cent rule takes away the incentive to trade, makes the WACR thin, pushes banks into building precautionary excess reserves, and forces more recourse to the MSF window. Some may argue that a 99 per cent daily floor is justified since banks, on average, maintain CRR balances significantly above the prescribed requirement. This, in fact, makes a case for a lower daily requirement, not higher. The issue is not how much banks maintain on average, but how best to ensure smooth arbitrage between the call-money market and CRR maintenance.  The last occasion when the RBI raised the minimum daily CRR maintenance to 99 per cent (from 70 per cent) was in July 2013. Then, however, it was a temporary squeeze to tighten liquidity conditions amid heightened volatility during the taper tantrum. Now it is to absorb a large surplus.  The current reduction in surplus is largely due to government cash balances of close to ₹7 trillion. Once the government spends, the surplus will rise again and the WACR may moderate from the current elevated level and possibly move below the policy rate. Hence the solution lies in addressing the durable liquidity surplus, which is expected to persist, through durable measures. Notably, there are limits to OMO sales and sell-buy swaps.  Though the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (Bank) scheme had stipulated that incremental deposits mobilised under the swap window would be exempt from the CRR/statutory liquidity ratio requirements, this does not prevent the RBI from subjecting all incremental net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) to the CRR or even raising the CRR on outstanding NDTL. A CRR increase is transparent, and it preserves price discovery and drains durable liquidity, leaving call volumes and the averaging mechanism intact.  Admittedly, the CRR is a cost to the banking system because the RBI does not pay any interest on its balances. However, we are in a period of large liquidity surplus and the cost of managing it also needs to be shared by the banking system. As of now, the RBI is bearing the entire cost. It would not be unreasonable if the banking system also bears a part of it.  Beyond cost sharing, there is a macroprudential case for a CRR increase. The CRR is now at a record low of 3.0 per cent. It is no longer a tool for day-to-day liquidity management. It is now a prudential buffer that can be deployed at short notice, even retrospectively, to inject liquidity in difficult times. It will also help build a buffer for future use.  In sum, it is important to durably align the WACR with the repo rate while preserving activity in the call-money market. If a durable surplus persists, as appears likely, raising the CRR from its historic low would be the most transparent and effective signal of durable tightening.

entry.title: Is a Chinese implosion looming?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Is a Chinese implosion looming?Is a Chinese implosion looming?

Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China

premium

China faces mounting economic and political challenges as slowing growth, declining tax revenues and concerns over leadership succession raise questions about its long-term stability.(Photo:PTI)

Navneeraj SharmaArvind Subramanian5 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 10:02 PM ISTThis has been an era of shocks. In the space of two decades, the world has witnessed globally disruptive wars — from Iraq in the 2000s to Ukraine and Iran today — a global financial crisis, a global pandemic, and a rogue American president upending the global order. Now, yet another potential shock must be addressed: Though few dare to speculate about it publicly, an economic and political perfect storm is bearing down on China.   On the political front, Chinese President Xi Jinping has ruthlessly eliminated all potential opposition and centralised power in his own hands. His decimation of the state, party, provincial, and military leadership has left a trail of bodies and resentment, even if the impenetrability of the Communist Party of China (CPC) makes this difficult to establish definitively. With blood and revenge hammering in their heads (to paraphrase Shakespeare), numerous humiliated and disgruntled former officials could make Xi’s succession, whenever it comes, disorderly. Cycles of apparent calm leading to chaos are not uncommon in Chinese history. They are intrinsic to what Francis Fukuyama has called the country’s “Bad Emperor” problem, with Mao Zedong and Xi representing the bad emperors of the Communist era.  On the economic front, the outlook is mixed, but downside risks are growing. Where some see an all-conquering powerhouse that is marrying technology to mass manufacturing, others see an economy that has been dragged into a structural slowdown by population ageing, a prolonged property market slump, rising youth unemployment, and growing hostility to private enterprise. Making matters worse, the longstanding source of Chinese dynamism — exports — is vulnerable to policy responses from the United States and Europe. But perhaps even more worrying is China’s fraying fiscal capacity. Warnings about unsustainable public debt are growing louder everywhere, but the situation in China is distinctive, owing to how it manages — or, rather, fails to manage — taxation.  Few states are as successful as China when it comes to surveilling and controlling the population. But taxes represent a reciprocal bargain with citizens, who accept expropriation as legitimate on the understanding that they will get something in return: Stability, public goods, improved standards of living, redistribution, and so forth. That is why wars and even empires can be lost when a state loses its capacity to tax its citizens.  The fate of the Ming and Qing dynasties is telling in this respect. Even discounting for the obvious historical differences, these episodes have faint echoes in developments today. We recently mapped China’s taxes and revenues since 1952. Two features stand out. First, and somewhat surprisingly, the CPC has not presided over a particularly strong fiscal state. Instead, it has raised a substantial share of resources without explicitly taxing its people. Until the late 1970s, about half the resources raised came from profits of state-owned enterprises (SOEs); and in the last two decades, about one-sixth (and as much as one-quarter at its peak in 2020) has come from land sales.  In other words, China has never managed to raise sufficient sums of money via personal income taxation, even during a period of extraordinary economic vibrancy. Over the last decade, its tax revenues from the personal-income tax averaged just 1.2 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP). Ironically, a communist state ideologically committed to collective ownership of the means of production has had to raise revenue by divesting itself of that most sacred input, land. Evidently, the CPC can make the Chinese cower in silence, but finds it difficult to reach into their pocketbooks.  The second and even more relevant finding is that, regardless of how they are measured, revenues and taxes have been declining for about a decade. For example, taxes (excluding social-insurance contributions) collapsed by nearly six percentage points between 2012 and 2025, from 18.4 per cent of GDP to 12.6 per cent. These are levels associated with a struggling, lower-middle-income country, not an aspiring superpower. It is difficult to say how much of this decline is attributable to growth falling below what headline figures indicate, and how much to weakening enforcement capacity. Either way, it seems that the government grew so reliant on nontax revenues that it found itself with no options when they dried up. Whether it can change course and impose taxes on the population very much remains to be seen.    The Chinese state could find itself triply exposed—to a succession crisis, a weakening economy, and a lack of resources to exercise power domestically and project it externally. In short, China’s entire growth and fiscal model, along with the social contract between the state and its citizens — coveted stability and material prosperity for restricted freedom and muzzled voice — may be in trouble.  Of course, any warning about China’s potential descent into disorder must contend with the CPC’s remarkable record of coercive control. A slow bleed of anaemic growth, rising restiveness, and deteriorating services is perhaps likelier. But even if the Chinese miracle ends with a whimper rather than a bang, the consequences may well be yet another global shock. 
  The writers are, respectively, an energy economist, and a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics ©Project Syndicate, 2026     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: CBAM: Let's get ready
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / CBAM: Let's get readyCBAM: Let's get ready

Sustained government support has to be given to MSMEs for them to achieve compliance with the UK and EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism systems

premium

India's exporters, particularly MSMEs, face growing compliance challenges as the UK and EU implement their Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) regulations. | Illustration : Binay Sinha

Amita Batra6 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 9:53 PM ISTIn a little over 60 days, the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) will be fully operational in both the United Kingdom (UK) and the European Union (EU). The CBAM is essentially aimed at bringing manufacturers/ exporters from non-UK/ EU countries on par with domestic producers in terms of carbon-price payment in these two economies, within the larger context of their green transition objectives.  This is particularly relevant for India, as the EU and the UK offer preferential market access through free trade agreements (FTAs) to our exporters in over 95 per cent tariff lines. The UK FTA is already in force, while the EU FTA is expected to be signed by the end of this year and become effective in 2027.  The UK CBAM covers five sectors — aluminum, cement, fertiliser, hydrogen, iron and steel. Unlike the EU, which had a year-long transition period during which only reporting obligations applied, the UK CBAM will enter the operational phase from January 1, 2027. The liability of the carbon-tax falls on the importer in the specified product categories above a certain value-based threshold level. Earlier this year, the UK accepted India’s Carbon Credit Trading System (CCTS) under its CBAM regulations, 2026. Consequently, the UK importer becomes eligible for carbon-price offset and the Indian exporter gets the benefit though price negotiation with the importer. However, to qualify for the offset, the importer has to fulfil the verification and paperwork requirements for the embodied emissions in the imported good. The accuracy and authenticity of the monitoring and measurement of embodied emissions, reporting, verification, and the actual costs incurred by the producer/exporter are crucial to availing of the benefits of the CCTS in the UK. Only a full member of the Global Accreditation Cooperation Incorporated is authorised to undertake and complete the data verification. If data on emissions is not available, default values will be used, which, being conservative estimates, will imply higher CBAM charges.   Many of India’s micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) may not have the necessary ability or resources to monitor and record embodied emissions and to sufficiently satisfy the requirement for hard and systematic evidence required by the UK authorities. Furthermore, India’s CCTS is nascent and will take time to develop. Therefore, the CCTS recognition by the UK may, at present, imply only a small discount for Indian exporters. To increase the depth of the carbon-credit market and strengthen the Indian exporters’ position in the UK market, the government needs to widen the sectoral coverage of CCTS and set more ambitious emission benchmarks for industry over a pre-defined timeline.  The EU CBAM is at present applicable to six sectors with electricity, in addition to the five in the case of the UK. However, a further expansion of the scope of the CBAM to cover over 180 downstream aluminium- and steel-intensive products is on the anvil. Also, whereas the UK uses emission intensity as the parameter for tax imposition, the EU CBAM is based on actual emissions data, direct and indirect, at a highly granular level along the supply chain.  In the UK, indirect emissions reporting has been postponed to 2029, at the earliest. Detailed mapping of the production value chain and corresponding emissions is therefore important, as reference default values will be specified by the EU Commission accordingly.  The data on emissions has to be verified by independent verifiers accredited by EU accreditation bodies. Accredited verifiers can start issuing verified reports on actual emissions in 2026 through the EU CBAM Registry from January 1, 2027. This will help finalise the actual verified emissions data for producers/ exporters rather than the use of default values. Purchase of certificates will begin from February 2027. The submission of the first annual CBAM declaration and surrender of corresponding certificates has to be done by September 2027. The CBAM tariff offset calculation will be based on accurate and valid carbon reduction certificates from the exporter’s home country. The year 2027 is, therefore, critical for CBAM implementation and for exporting countries to be compliance-ready.  Given that strict scrutiny and adherence to the norms under CBAM regulations are to be expected in both the EU and the UK, Indian exporters, especially small and medium-sized enterprises, will need government support to make the most of our FTAs with these two economies. Towards this end, the following measures may be useful.  Firstly, the government or the industry chambers need to undertake a product code matching exercise separately with the UK and the EU CBAM’s current and potential product lists. This will help manufacturers/exporters gain clarity on the extent of their tax liability under CBAM, as granular-level product specifications may not correspond across countries.  Secondly, detailed mapping of carbon emissions along the entire production value chain may be beyond MSMEs in India. Even most medium enterprises may not yet have the necessary metering or accounting systems to track carbon emissions for upstream or downstream value chains.  The Securities and Exchange Board of India’s expansion of the Scope 3 level (indirect/value-chain carbon emissions) reporting requirement to the top 1,000 listed companies from financial year 2026-27 is a step in the right direction. However, as it is a voluntary requirement, it may not necessarily prepare Indian producers/ exporters for the mandatory data obligations under the EU CBAM. In fact, for MSMEs, even scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting is voluntary. This makes getting carbon emissions data along the value chain difficult, even for large listed companies. It will, therefore, be useful if budgetary support is specifically delineated for CBAM infrastructure schemes, besides incentives and initiatives to encourage greener production methods. In addition, bilateral discussions at the Trade and Technology Council meetings with the EU should include negotiations on technology sharing and financial support, in line with India’s demands in international climate negotiations.  Thirdly, a complete match between the Indian carbon-emission accounting framework and the respective UK and EU systems will need to be established. This should be taken up either by the government or at the level of industry chambers and exporter associations. The MSMEs also need to be sufficiently familiarised with the respective emission accounting frameworks and methodologies, and suitably trained to provide accurate data in both CBAM formats.   Therefore, recognising that the strict implementation of CBAM is a fast-approaching inevitability in the UK and the EU, making Indian exporters compliance-ready is an immediate necessity.  
 The writer is professor, School of International Studies, JNU, and author of India’s Trade Policy in the 21st Century, Routledge: London, 2022. entry.title: When tariff walls become a ladder
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / When tariff walls become a ladderWhen tariff walls become a ladder

Tariffs, wars and global disorder are forging a more resilient India Inc

premium

Exporters are taking the shock on the chin, not treating trade friction as an impassable wall, but as a mirror reflecting the need for structural reform (Representative Image)

Sachchidanand Shukla5 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:58 PM ISTIndia is roughly 3 per cent of global gross domestic product (GDP) but nearly 20 per cent of its population. The arithmetic carries a hard truth: India’s next phase of growth cannot rely on the domestic market alone. It must win market share abroad by building businesses that can dominate internationally.  Paradoxically, Donald Trump’s trade offensive may, in fact, be helping. Corporate India is increasingly choosing grit over grievance. Exporters are taking the shock on the chin, not treating trade friction as an impassable wall, but as a mirror reflecting the need for structural reform. This baptism by trade fire is accelerating a long-overdue shift from cheap volume arbitrage towards complex manufacturing, scalar capabilities, research & development (R&D) and potentially towards proprietary brands.  The petroleum-refining sector that prompted US Secretary of State Marco Rubio to call India a “refining superpower” is a case in point. It illustrates resilience through scale, sophistication and market optionality. With capacity of roughly 258 million tonnes a year, and output capable of running above nameplate capacity, India imports crude, adds value through complex refining, and exports diesel, petrol, aviation fuel and naphtha to markets including the EU and even Russia. Redirecting cargoes while meeting domestic demand has strengthened energy security, foreign-exchange earnings and India’s ability to absorb geopolitical disruption.  Pharmaceuticals also show the stakes. Washington’s proposed framework — a phased duty of 100 per cent on imported generic medicines, escalating to 200 per cent  — strikes at the economics of an industry that sells 41 per cent of its generic-formulation exports to the US market. Yet, Indian drugmakers are not abandoning the world’s largest health care market. The tariff threat has made the shift from commodity generics to high-value innovation a corporate imperative.  Sun Pharma’s $11.8-billion acquisition of Organon; Lupin’s commitment of $250 million in Florida to local manufacturing and R&D are recent examples. Of about $20.5 billion in US investment pledges announced by Indian leaders at the SelectUSA summit, $19 billion came from pharma. The model is moving from exporting to onshore, high-value manufacturing and speciality drugs.  Clean energy tells a similar story. When the US imposed a preliminary 126 per cent countervailing duty on Indian solar-cell imports, the companies did not shrink capacity. They redirected volumes towards Europe and West Asia, while using the production-linked incentive scheme to move into high-efficiency modules. Rather than remain dependent on raw cell exports, firms are climbing the supply chain through module assembly and local manufacturing abroad.  In the second quarter of 2026-27, export performance reinforces the broader point. Merchandise exports rose 18 per cent year-on-year (YoY) to $260 billion, one of the fastest increases since 2023, while goods-and-services exports increased 14 per cent to $476 billion. Petroleum-product exports rose 32 per cent YoY in September, keeping up its stellar growth rate through first half of the year. True, there is an element of higher prices accounting for a bulk of this growth, as against volume increase. Total exports expanded from $498 billion in FY21 to a record $863 billion in FY26, with a significant pivot from agricultural commodities, gems and textiles towards technology-intensive production and specialised services.  Importantly, the export basket now looks materially different. Electronics that clocked 70 per cent YoY growth in September rose from $11 billion in FY21 to $48 billion in FY26, lifting its share in merchandise exports from a low single-digit to 10.8 per cent. Engineering goods exceed 26 per cent of shipments, helping push non-petroleum exports to $388 billion.  The $421-billion services sector is moving beyond routine IT support into consulting, finance and engineering design. Threats of border taxes on cross-border data flows and tightening visa rules are dismantling the legacy business model of cheap headcount arbitrage. The industry heavyweights are transforming offshore delivery centres into specialised hubs dedicated to enterprise AI, Cloud architecture, and cybersecurity, embedding themselves deeply into global corporate infrastructures.   To hedge against single-market regulatory shocks, tech giants are simultaneously expanding nearshore delivery networks across Latam and Eastern Europe. EU exports reached $86 billion, with deeper reach into France, Italy and the Czech Republic. New corridors across West Africa and Southern Africa are carrying pharmaceuticals, automobiles and industrial machinery. Trade deals, commercial diplomacy and China+1 realignments are reinforcing this shift. Agreements with the EU, the UK, Australia, New Zealand and Oman widen preferential access for goods and open channels for services.  But tariffs do not automatically create competitiveness. They can destroy margins, displace workers and expose weak balance sheets. India must use external pressure to accelerate reforms it needed anyway — namely, lower logistics costs, predictable regulation, reliable infrastructure, deeper skills and patient capital.  The American tariff offensive was meant to assert leverage and pull supply chains home. It is instead hastening the growth and industrial evolution of America’s most consequential democratic global partner. For India, doubling from 3 per cent of global GDP and ultimately to 10 per cent, will require more than merely exporting more; it will require creating capabilities and franchises the world cannot easily replace.  Indian enterprise should trade volume for value — and policymakers must sustain a diversified, multipolar trade architecture. The ultimate irony will then be clear: Protectionism intended as a wall will have become a ladder, lifting a more resilient India, even if belatedly, towards the centre of global commerce.

entry.title: The new rules of cybersecurity
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The new rules of cybersecurityThe new rules of cybersecurity

Beyond compliance, regulations must prioritise speed and preparedness in responding to threats in the AI age

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Ajay TyagiBasu Chandola5 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:48 PM ISTIn July, AI agents undergoing cybersecurity evaluations at OpenAI circumvented restrictions on internet access and compromised systems belonging to Hugging Face, an external artificial intelligence (AI) platform. The incident highlighted an emerging cybersecurity challenge: Increasingly capable AI systems can identify and exploit vulnerabilities without direct human instructions.  As AI becomes integrated into critical digital infrastructure, these developments raise questions about the adequacy of existing cybersecurity frameworks. With AI enabling faster identification and exploitation of vulnerabilities, cybersecurity regulations must place greater emphasis on operational resilience.  AI is changing the cybersecurity ecosystem in two distinct ways. First, it can strengthen cybersecurity through vulnerability detection, network monitoring, and automated incident response, while enabling malicious actors to identify and exploit weaknesses more efficiently. Second, AI systems themselves introduce vulnerabilities. Techniques such as prompt injection can manipulate models through untrusted inputs, while autonomous agents can access external tools, databases, and operational systems. Weaknesses in the controls governing such access could have consequences beyond the AI application itself.  Recent advisories from India’s Computer Emergency Response Team (Cert-In) demonstrate the relevance of these concerns. In October, Cert-In reported incidents of AI agents undergoing evaluation accessing systems belonging to Indian organisations without authorisation. The affected organisations had not detected the intrusions themselves; the incidents were disclosed by AI model providers. Cert-In separately reported financially motivated campaigns involving agentic AI tools, where automation cut the time between initial compromise and impact from days to hours.  Another incident involving India’s digital certification provider eMudhra illustrates these challenges. On October 17, an independent researcher identified weak cryptographic keys associated with eight intermediate certificates, potentially using AI-assisted techniques, according to eMudhra. The vulnerabilities could have allowed attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites, prompting major browser providers to block the affected certificates. Significantly, the weaknesses had remained undetected despite independent audits.  These incidents highlight an important distinction. Many vulnerabilities remain conventional, including exposed credentials and inadequate access controls. However, AI can speed up their identification and exploitation, leaving organisations less time to respond. Cybersecurity approaches relying primarily on periodic audits, vulnerability assessments and scheduled remediation may, therefore, become insufficient.  India has an established cybersecurity architecture comprising legal, institutional and sector-specific mechanisms. The Information Technology Act, 2000, provides the legislative foundation, with Cert-In serving as the national agency for cybersecurity incident response and National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre responsible for protecting critical information infrastructure.   Cert-In’s directions also mandate reporting specified cybersecurity incidents within six hours, while the National Cyber Coordination Centre facilitates threat-intelligence sharing. These mechanisms are complemented by cybersecurity requirements introduced by sectoral regulators. The challenge is to ensure that this architecture remains effective against AI-related threats, particularly as attacks become faster and more sophisticated. Cert-In’s May 2026 blueprint recommends continuous vulnerability management, AI-aware monitoring and stronger incident-response capabilities. However, operational preparedness remains uneven. A 2025 study by the Data Security Council of India and Palo Alto Networks found that nearly 79 per cent of surveyed respondents planned to integrate AI into cybersecurity operations, while only around 8 per cent reported full integration.  India’s financial regulators offer examples of how cybersecurity principles can be translated into institutional responsibilities and measurable requirements. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) directions on IT governance establish board-level responsibility for technology risks, information security, and business continuity. Its cybersecurity directions for non-bank payment system operators also address application security, third-party dependencies and incident response. The RBI’s FREE-AI Committee report adds recommendations for responsible AI adoption in finance.  The Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) has adopted a more measurable approach. Its 2024 Cybersecurity and Cyber Resilience Framework introduced a Cyber Capability Index based on 23 weighted parameters, alongside periodic assessments for larger regulated entities. It provides for shared security operations centres to support smaller institutions. More recently, Sebi established a task force in response to advanced AI vulnerability-detection tools, to coordinate threat intelligence, vulnerability management and assessment of third-party risks. As AI changes the nature of cyber risks, the challenge is to adapt these arrangements rather than build a parallel regulatory system. Four priorities follow.  First, sectoral regulators should require cybersecurity assessments of AI systems deployed in critical sectors, both before deployment and following significant updates. These assessments should cover models, connected applications, credentials and agent permissions, including testing for unauthorised access and actions. Cert-In could develop common testing protocols, with independent evaluations for high-risk deployments.  Second, regulators should add measurable cyber resilience indicators to existing compliance requirements. Drawing on Sebi’s Cyber Capability Index, assessments could track the time taken to detect intrusions, contain compromised systems, revoke unauthorised access and restore critical services. These should be supported by regular simulation exercises and continuous vulnerability monitoring.  Third, Cert-In should establish a formal coordination mechanism with critical infrastructure authorities and sectoral regulators. This mechanism could develop common standards for classifying and reporting AI-related cybersecurity incidents, facilitate timely threat-intelligence sharing and coordinate responses to vulnerabilities affecting multiple organisations. Sectoral guidelines should also clarify the responsibilities of AI developers, deployers and third-party service providers, particularly where incidents arise from autonomous AI systems or shared technological infrastructure.  Fourth, India should prioritise operationalising the IndiaAI Safety Institute to strengthen cybersecurity testing and evaluation. The Institute could develop common standards for assessing vulnerabilities in AI models and autonomous agents, and establish shared testing facilities. These assessments could inform Cert-In and sectoral regulators in developing measurable requirements for AI-related cyber resilience.  India’s forthcoming consultation on AI regulation provides an opportunity to assess these issues.  The broader lesson is relevant beyond India. Existing cybersecurity regulations remain necessary, but their effectiveness will increasingly depend on how well they account for the changing speed and scale  of cyber threats. As AI becomes embedded in critical systems, cybersecurity governance must move beyond procedural compliance towards ensuring that institutions can anticipate, withstand, contain, and recover from emerging risks.          
The writers are, respectively, former chairman of Sebi and associate fellow at Observer Research Foundation     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Risk of irrelevance?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Risk of irrelevance?Risk of irrelevance?

The scale of the selling and the speed and magnitude of the underperformance in Indian equities are unsustainable

premium

Foreign portfolio investors have withdrawn $65 billion from Indian equities since September 2024, amid sharp market underperformance and declining global investor interest. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Akash Prakash6 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 12:19 AM ISTI have been investing in Indian equities for over 30 years. Rarely have I seen foreign sentiment this bad. India no longer features in global conversations. What I am saying is not new. Since the Indian market’s peak in September 2024, we have seen $65 billion in net outflows by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). Over the last decade, India has received zero net-foreign flows.  The stock of Indian equities owned by foreigners has fallen from $930 billion to about $675 billion, and foreign ownership as a percentage of the market is now at a 15-year low. India is now a consensus underweight for all global investors and our weighting itself has shrunk from 21 per cent in September 2024 to about 10 per cent today (MSCI Emerging Market index).  One company, TSMC, has a benchmark weight 50 per cent higher than that of all of India! The three EM heavyweights — TSMC, Samsung Electronics, and SK Hynix — together account for 30 per cent of the index, but have almost three times India’s weighting.  We have also seen unprecedented underperformance. Since the peak in September 2024, Indian equities are down about 25 per cent in dollar terms, even as the EM indices are up about 50 per cent. We have, therefore, underperformed by 7,500 basis points (75 percentage points) in the last two years alone. I have never in my career seen this quantum of underperformance in this short a period. It has destroyed careers and blown up funds. There are numerous funds that have destroyed 10-year track records in the last 24 months by simply being overweight India.  Normally, I would look at these statistics and numbers as contrarian indicators. This is exactly why I would argue — and still do — that we will soon see a turnaround in India’s relative and absolute performance. The scale of the selling and the speed and magnitude of the underperformance are unsustainable. How can three companies in Asia have three times the index weight of a country with India’s size and potential?  How can these three companies have a combined index weight of 30 per cent, almost identical to the combined weight of India and China, at 30.5 per cent? Something is clearly wrong. It seems ludicrous that three Asian technology companies can have an index weight almost equivalent to 40 per cent of the world’s population. A classic contrarian indicator, if there ever was one.  However, what troubles me is that for the first time I am now being asked about the need for an India-dedicated allocation. Many allocators no longer think India is important enough to warrant dedicated exposure. Why bother with sticking their neck out and betting on India specifically, especially given the extent of underperformance. This conversation has come up now after years. Twenty years ago, every allocator had dedicated money in China and Brazil, and India was a debate. Over time, it became conventional wisdom that to invest in EM, you needed dedicated pools of capital for India, greater China and Brazil. If allocators are now unwilling to make an India-specific bet, it is a big negative and will constrain the quantum of foreign equity as well as the diversity of capital into the country. Non-dedicated exposure by definition is more cyclical.  So why this change in thinking? First of all, it is the decline in India’s EM weighting. At only 10 per cent, we are half what we used to be and three countries — Taiwan, Korea and China — are 70 per cent of the EM index. Do you really need to bother with India? Even getting India wrong will not really move the needle. Over the last 10 years, India has anyway underperformed the EM indices by about 180 basis points annually. Even on a 20-year basis, India has just marginally outperformed. The narrative that you need to be in India because of the quality of companies, sustainability of growth and entrepreneurial energy is getting lost. There is fundamentally less belief that we have decades of strong growth ahead of us.  Second, many investors have come to the conclusion that India may not deliver enough absolute returns. Their calculations are as follows. The Nifty index in rupees has delivered about 10.5 per cent per annum over the last 20 years. Assuming a capital gains tax impact of about 15 per cent (the average of the short-term rate of 20 per cent and the long-term rate of 12.5 per cent), this brings the return down to about 8.9 per cent. Then, assuming a near 4 per cent rupee depreciation (the average over the last 20 years), this brings the return down to about 6 per cent in dollar terms.  Why bother with 6 per cent when the 100-year annualised returns in US equities are about 10 per cent? I would argue that 25-year Nifty returns are near 13.5 per cent not 10 per cent. Nifty returns understate market returns and assuming continued 4 per cent currency depreciation makes no sense given the narrowing inflation differentials. Also, given the valuations, can you assume continued 10 per cent compounding in the United States? However, it does not matter what I think, this is what investors are saying.  All allocators are upset about the capital gains tax. They do not pay these taxes in any other major jurisdiction. It drops projected long-term annualised returns by about 2 per cent and that is a huge difference when comparing countries over long holding periods. There is also the perception that India remains a complex place to do business. Indian service providers do a good job of scaring the risk and compliance teams of global investors. While this may be unfair, the perception sticks.  India is also seen as the biggest global loser from artificial intelligence (AI), as our key advantages of demographics and a skilled white-collar workforce lose relevance in an AI-first world. Innovation and research & development, which are driving value creation globally, are seen as areas of weakness in India. One can refute this argument, but many allocators believe it.  India is also caught in a no-man’s land, not cheap enough for value investors to pile in but not growing fast enough to attract growth investors either.  If India were to lose its attraction as an independent asset class that is a cause of worry. We will attract less structural capital and be of less relevance to global allocators. Not a good place to be for a country fundamentally short of capital. Equity markets are a competitive advantage for India, we weaken this if we lose access to dedicated pools of long-term capital.  I remain convinced that all this data is more a contrarian indicator and not a reason to turn more negative on India. Much of this is cyclical and the tide will turn. However, we must guard against slipping further down the investor consideration set in the meantime.  
           The writer is with Amansa Capital   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Advance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implications
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Advance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implicationsAdvance Authorisation: Job work abroad and its key tax implications

Experts clarify rules on overseas job work under advance authorisation, leasing capital goods under EPCG and timelines for invoicing and export shipments

premium

Exporters must comply with customs and GST rules for overseas job work and shipments (Representative Image)

TNC Rajagopalan3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 12:05 AM ISTWe have an export order for an item. We have imported the materials required for manufacturing the item duty free under an advance authorisation. One of our machines to carry out a specialised process has broken down. It will take quite some time to send the machine abroad for repairs and get it back. Our customer cannot wait that long. So, we want to send the imported duty-free material abroad to get the specialised process done and re-import it for further manufacture at our factory. We refer to Paragraph 4.33 of the Handbook of Procedures (HBP), which allows the endorsement of the name of the supporting manufacturer in an advance authorisation. Can we get endorsement of the name of a supporting manufacturer abroad and if so, what are the tax implications?  Para 4.33 of the HBP does not expressly restrict endorsement only to supporting manufacturers or job workers located in India. You can therefore seek endorsement of the overseas job worker’s name and address, explaining that the materials will return to India for further manufacture and subsequent export towards discharge of the export obligation. The proviso to condition (xii) of notification number 21/2023-Customs permits transfer of imported materials for job work subject to the relevant GST (Goods and Services Tax) conditions. Those provisions do not expressly prohibit overseas job work. You should comply with the applicable job-work-challan, recordkeeping, reporting and return-period requirements, and declare the purpose of the temporary export in the shipping bill. On re-import, the processed goods will attract duty under Section 20 of the Customs Act, 1962, read with any applicable exemption notification. The original duty-free import under the Advance Authorisation does not necessarily exempt this re-import. The invoice of the foreign job-worker will not attract IGST on reverse charge basis because where the specialized process is performed entirely abroad on goods physically made available to the foreign job worker, the place of supply is outside the taxable territory in accordance with Section 13(3)(a) of the IGST Act, 2017.  In the previous Foreign Trade Policy (FTP), capital goods could be imported under Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) even if the same were financed by a leasing company. In the current FTP 2023, there is no such provision. Can we import capital goods on lease basis and clear under EPCG scheme even in current policy 2023?  Para 2.33 of the FTP permits import of capital goods under lease financing without specific DGFT permission. Also, the current definition of ‘importer’ in the Customs Act, 1962 covers the lessee even for import under the EPCG scheme.  Our customer wants us to raise the invoice but delay export shipment by two months. Can we do that?  Yes. Section 31(1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax (CGST) Act, 2017 requires you to raise the invoice before or at the time of removal. However, Rule 96A of the CGST Rules, 2017 requires you to export the goods removed under Letter of Undertaking or bond within three months from the date of invoice (not removal from the factory). The Commissioner may extend the period.

entry.title: Uneasy lies the governance space
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Uneasy lies the governance spaceUneasy lies the governance space

The ripples the Tata affair will cause are yet to become clear - but promoters will be nervous at such a coup by the professional hire

premium

The governance tensions at Tata Sons have raised questions about promoter control, board independence and the balance of power between shareholders and professional management. | Photo: File

Rama Bijapurkar5 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 10:05 PM ISTL’affaire Tata Sons has brought into focus the uneasy space between promoters, professional managers, and boards, that India Inc constantly negotiates. While there has not been much public comment from India Inc on the situation (and this columnist rushes in where angels fear to tread), there has been enormous private speculation about how this situation came to pass, and nervous conjecture on what the ripple effects of this will be in shaping the future governance space.   This is neither a spat among shareholder groups for control, nor a summary sacking of a chief executive officer by a promoter. We have seen those movies before. This is almost the first time that a professional manager-CEO, with the board on his side and non-shareholder government institutions weighing in, has sought to marginalise a 66 per cent-owning promoter in decision choices that impact not just the direction of the business (though we are not explicitly hearing from either side about strategic fault lines), but also the promoter’s shareholding.   While CEOs pushing back publicly and openly fighting shareholders is common in bastions of capitalism like the United States, with widely distributed shareholding and boards playing a greater fiduciary role, in India such battles are rare, especially if it is a promoter shareholder. Indian promoters hold the hallowed place of a company’s birth parents with special rights and responsibilities — some enshrined in law, others in culture.   ITC and Larsen & Toubro (L&T) are two unforgettable examples in India of CEO-shareholder battles. In the case of ITC, the battle was against promoter BAT’s  (British American Tobacco’s) move to gain control of the company and stop diversification, while in the case of L&T, it was against a dominant shareholder group, with the CEO fighting to retain management control. In both cases, the government backed the CEO, but by weighing in through its 30 to 40 per cent shareholding via financial institutions it controlled, keeping within the legitimate norm of capitalism: Jiski lathi, uski bhains (whoever has the stick owns the buffalo).   What makes the present Tata Sons case different is that government-controlled entities do not own large chunks of shares, and the duelling ground is not an annual general meeting or extraordinary general meeting. That a CEO with no shareholding backing, along with board members who do not represent chunks of shareholding, can challenge a promoter with a 66 per cent holding and pressure it to dilute its stake, and not have sway over decisions is a first-time challenge to power structures — which have stood the test of time, tradition, convention, and culture, rightly or wrongly. It brings a fresh round of calibration, especially by promoters, of their terms of endearment and engagement with professional CEOs, not to mention boards. More so, if their shareholding is well below 51 per cent.  The relationship between professional managers and promoters in India has always had a degree of tension. The differences that typically end in the CEO quitting could be on several dimensions —differences in direction, risk appetite and prudence, business ambition, remuneration (less so of late as CEO salaries and stock options have zoomed upwards) and often over different perceptions of where the power to make what kind of decisions rests — the birth parent or the foster parent. Human resources consultants frequently counsel boards and CEOs that once the chemistry with the promoter has gone sour, there is no salvaging the relationship.   The separation of management from ownership is not common in India yet, though nascent examples are emerging. Big stock market influencers welcome owner presence in management because they feel a reassuring common focus on increasing shareholder value.  Many employees also prefer a promoter at the helm, seeing this as offering more predictability and benevolence than the CEO or the board of the day. Even in a company like Infosys,  set up by professionals, the “founders” (as they preferred to be called) took turns in running the company in accordance with their pre-agreed plan. The board went along with the frequent changes at the top, presumably because these were the promoters who had built an amazing company and it seemed only fair that they each had their turn.   Given the promoter-friendly, promoter-respectful and promoter-on-top ethos of corporate governance that has existed and continues to exist in India, this departure from the norm against none other than the venerated, iconic Tata promoter group with its track record of trusteeship and larger good over personal gain has rocked the comfort boat all around.  The ripples it will cause are yet to become clear — will promoters be nervous seeing such a coup by the professional hire? How will they respond? Will they pick boards like in the old days, based on loyalty and narrow subject-matter expertise? Especially as the law of the land and the market regulator push more power and accountability in the hands of independent directors? Will boards be now placed under more pressure from external directives on which way to vote, getting trapped between the rock and the hard place of the promoter and the proverbial hand of God? Will CEOs have less freedom to operate and more fetters? And does this add to the bad rap that India has been getting of late as a safe, stable place to invest in for the long term? Probably yes to all.  Since one big pillar of the argument is the national and systemic importance of Tata Sons, its board perhaps needs to be more transparent on the rationale for its many volte-faces.
