entry.title: Making sense of street signs
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Making sense of street signsMaking sense of street signs

FPI selling is driven mostly by global factors

premium

Foreign portfolio investors have sold Indian equities worth over ₹2.9 trillion so far this year, weighing on the Nifty 50, even as strong domestic institutional inflows have supported the market.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:24 PM ISTThe performance of the Indian stock markets is being intensely debated. The benchmark Nifty 50 is down over 12 per cent since the beginning of the year. Expectedly, various aspects of the issue were extensively discussed at the annual Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit, which ended on Wednesday. One of the biggest reasons for the Indian stock markets’ underperformance is relentless selling by foreign portfolio investors (FPIs). At a net level, they sold stocks worth over ₹2.9 trillion so far this year.  There are several reasons why FPIs are selling Indian stocks, the biggest being the artificial-intelligence (AI) trade. Some analysts have also pointed out the difficulties that FPIs tend to face in the Indian markets.  In this regard, Securities and Exchange Board of India Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey noted at the summit that the regulator was engaged with FPIs from across the world. There are some issues, and the regulator is working on them. The time taken for registering an FPI, for instance, has declined significantly. In the broader context, Mr Pandey also highlighted that market capitalisation as a share of gross domestic product had increased from about 69 per cent in 2015-16 to about 130 per cent this financial year. Clearly, the increase has been driven mostly by new listings and not necessarily by valuation expansion. In fact, valuations have been significantly compressed in recent periods.  As was pointed out at the summit, in terms of the number of initial public offerings (IPOs), India was at the top of the charts globally in 2025 and ranked number three in terms of value. Significant activity is being witnessed this year as well. Notably, Jio Platforms, which had the biggest IPO, was listed this week at a significant premium and became the second-most valuable company on the Indian exchanges. The Jio IPO and its listing highlight another layer in the ongoing market debate. Despite the broader trend, demand for the IPO, including from FPIs, and its successful listing clearly show that the Indian market is capable of providing risk capital at scale to strong businesses. This has been made possible partly by sustained increases in participation by domestic investors, including through mutual funds. Domestic institutional investors have bought stocks worth over ₹7 trillion since the beginning of this year.  At a fundamental level, as analysts have rightly pointed out, not much has changed for the Indian markets. The economy is growing strongly and there isn’t much to complain about the incoming corporate results for the second quarter this financial year. Thus, FPI selling is being driven largely by global factors. Besides the increased investment in AI-related companies, risk aversion owing to geopolitical uncertainties has also affected foreign flows. Further, rising bond yields in developed countries and currency-market volatility are complicating investment calculations for global fund managers. Nonetheless, there are issues that India must debate and address. FPIs compare post-tax dollar returns in various jurisdictions, which tends to adversely affect India allocation. Thus, there is a need to align India’s tax policy with global best practices. While the stock markets have gained depth, India still needs foreign capital to supplement domestic savings. Another aspect worth debating is how different instruments are taxed for resident Indian investors. It is being argued that lower taxes on equity are pushing households to the stock markets. There are various ways of bringing parity.   Topics : Sensex Nifty BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Indian stock markets

entry.title: Building empowered cities
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Building empowered citiesBuilding empowered cities

Strong local governments are essential for sustained growth

premium

With India's urban population projected to reach 850 million by 2050, stronger municipal governance, greater financial autonomy and effective devolution of powers will be crucial for sustainable urban development.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 10:35 PM ISTIndia’s ability to sustain rapid economic growth will increasingly depend on how well its cities are governed. With the urban population projected to rise from around 500 million currently to 850 million by 2050, the pressure on housing, transport and basic services will intensify. In this context, NITI Aayog member Rajiv Gauba recently argued for a fundamental change in how cities were planned, governed and financed. His observation that cities cannot be governed from state capitals underlines a fundamental weakness in India’s urban governance framework — the lack of autonomy for urban local bodies (ULBs). A recent NITI Aayog report titled “Moving Towards Effective City Government” highlighted weak devolution, fragmented responsibilities, and inadequate municipal finances. The 74th constitutional amendment, which intended to strengthen local self-government, remains incomplete. Although the Constitution lists 18 functions for possible devolution, responsibilities such as urban planning, water supply, transport and sanitation are often divided among municipal corporations, state departments, and specialised agencies.  Political leadership is equally constrained. Mayors often lack executive and financial powers, while municipal commissioners exercise substantial administrative authority and may be transferred frequently. Besides, as a Comptroller and Auditor General study published in 2024 has found, municipal elections were delayed in more than 61 per cent of ULBs across 17 audited states. Short mayoral tenures and delayed elections weaken continuity, making long-term planning difficult. This is a serious drawback and must be addressed. India has increased investment in urban infrastructure in recent years. The budgetary outlay for the urban sector has grown substantially over the years. The ₹1 trillion Urban Challenge Fund, announced in the 2025-26 Union Budget, and allocations of ₹5,000 crore each for seven city-economic regions over five years seek to strengthen cities as growth hubs. However, infrastructure spending alone cannot deliver better outcomes without capable local institutions. Municipalities need trained personnel, effective coordination among service agencies, and greater authority to respond to local needs.  Further, weak finances restrict municipal autonomy. A Reserve Bank of India report (2024), covering 232 municipal corporations, found that their own revenues remained inadequate to meet routine expenditure. Improving property-tax assessments, expanding digital land records, and strengthening user-charge collection can help cities mobilise their own resources. State Finance Commissions must be constituted on time, and their recommendations implemented transparently. The 16th Finance Commission’s increased grants to urban local governments provide an opportunity, but transfers alone cannot improve service delivery unless municipalities have the capacity to use funds effectively. Reforms can begin with million-plus cities before being extended to smaller urban centres. These cities have established institutions and a greater capacity to implement changes, making them suitable starting points. India’s urban challenge is not simply to build more infrastructure but to ensure that cities can manage it effectively. States must devolve responsibilities along with adequate funds, staff and decision-making powers. Empowered and accountable municipal governments are essential in improving living standards, attracting investment, and ensuring that urbanisation supports sustained economic growth.   Topics : Urban governance BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment financial management at local body

entry.title: Gendered skill gap
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Gendered skill gapGendered skill gap

Women face multiple employment-related constraints

premium

Women’s participation in apprenticeship programmes has increased, but gender gaps in technical skills, employment opportunities and unpaid caregiving continue to limit access to better-paying jobs.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 10:16 PM ISTThe latest data on the National Apprenticeship Promotion Scheme (NAPS) points to a familiar problem in India’s labour market: Women are entering the workforce in greater numbers, but their access to skilled and better-paying occupations remains limited. Women account for 29.5 per cent of the 1.35 million apprentices engaged under the NAPS in 2026-27 so far. This is a substantial improvement over the 11.8 per cent in 2018-19 and 22.5 per cent in 2024-25, although it is below the 32.4 per cent recorded in 2025-26. The more revealing numbers, however, are by trade. Women account for only 6 per cent of electricians and 2.6 per cent of fitters, and trades such as welding, diesel mechanics, and lineman have had no women apprentices. The government has sought to address this through apprenticeship fairs and stakeholder consultations, and by encouraging women to enter a wider range of sectors. The NAPS provides structured, industry-linked, on-the-job training, with the government covering 25 per cent of the prescribed minimum stipend, subject to a ceiling of ₹1,500 a month under NAPS-2. Yet the persistence of occupational segregation suggests that mobilisation alone will not suffice.  This matters because the challenge facing women is no longer simply whether they participate in economic activities but the quality and sustainability of that participation. The female labour force participation rate among women aged 15 years and above has risen to 40 per cent. This is encouraging, but employment statistics can conceal substantial differences in economic security and agency. In rural India, 32.9 per cent of female workers are helpers in household enterprises, while only 9.3 per cent are in regular wage or salaried employment. Such work counts as employment but may not provide an independent income. The high incidence of self-employment also raises concerns about whether it reflects genuine opportunities or constrained choices, and whether it allows women to accumulate skills, assets and earnings. In the age group 15-59, among those who had received formal vocational or technical training, only 51.4 per cent of women were employed, compared with 83.3 per cent of men. Thus, training alone clearly does not guarantee employment. The transition from training to work depends on accessible vacancies, safe mobility, workplace conditions, employer attitudes and family responsibilities. Occupational segregation compounds the problem. If women are channelled into a narrow range of services or low-skilled occupations while remaining absent from technical trades, their opportunities for higher productivity and earnings remain restricted.  However, constraints for women are not entirely workplace-related. Women aged 15-59 spend an average of 140 minutes a day on unpaid caregiving, compared with 74 minutes for men. Time poverty can push women towards work that is close to home, flexible or home-based, even when better opportunities exist elsewhere. The result can be interrupted careers and weaker lifetime earnings. Concern about safety and harassment further affects women’s willingness and ability to take up jobs involving travel, shifts or male-dominated workplaces. Digital exclusion adds another barrier. Policy must consequently move beyond counting female entrants. Apprenticeship programmes should track women’s participation across occupations, completion and placement rates, wages and progression after training. Expanding childcare, safe transport, affordable accommodation and effective workplace-grievance mechanisms is equally important.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment women employment gender gap women empowerment labour market

entry.title: Growth with resilience
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Growth with resilienceGrowth with resilience

Vibrant BFSI sector will augment growth

premium

India's resilient economic growth and improving banking-sector health highlight the BFSI sector's crucial role in financing investment, infrastructure and long-term development.

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 28 2026 | 10:11 PM ISTThe three-day annual Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit, which ended on Wednesday, brought together policymakers, financial-sector regulators, industry leaders and investors to discuss the current state of the economy and the financial sector, as well as future challenges and opportunities. Given the backdrop of heightened global economic uncertainty and varied risks faced by different countries, the summit provided a robust assessment of the current situation. One recurring theme in the talks delivered by policymakers and in discussions was the resilience being displayed by the Indian economy even in adverse circumstances. Indeed, India is growing rapidly despite uncertainties. The Indian economy surprised analysts by posting a growth rate of 7.8 per cent in the first quarter this financial year. The International Monetary Fund recognised this, increasing India’s growth projection for the current year to 7 per cent, as against its previous forecast of 6.4 per cent.  The banking, financial services, and insurance (BFSI) sector plays an important role in the development of any economy.  It helps channel surplus savings in the system into productive investment, which enables growth, jobs, and wealth creation. The health and efficiency of the financial sector also play a vital role in serving the needs of the economy and enabling it to attain its true potential. Given that India is seen as largely a bank-financed economy, it is worth noting — as was also underscored at the summit by Shaktikanta Das, Principal Secretary-2 to the Prime Minister and former Governor of the Reserve Bank of India — that the health of Indian banking has consistently improved over the past several years, with the gross non-performing asset ratio in the banking system declining to a multi-decade low of 1.8 per cent of its gross advances in March. The financial position of the Indian corporate sector is also strong. India has clearly overcome the so-called twin balance-sheet problem of the last decade and is ready to invest — initial signs of this are now beginning to emerge. Mr Das also noted: “The BFSI sector has to take the lead in financing large infrastructure and new-age manufacturing to support massive public and private asset creation.”  India has a vibrant financial sector and its sustained development will be critical to attaining higher growth over the medium to long term. The development of the pension and insurance sector, for instance, will increase the availability of  long-term funds for long-gestation projects. India already has a robust equity market, which is capable of providing risk capital to businesses even in an uncertain global economic environment. This has been made possible partly by the increasing penetration of mutual funds and the trust of the household sector in the market. However, in a large, vibrant, and complex market economy, economic agents have varied needs that the financial sector should be able to meet. It must be capable of providing timely credit to small businesses as well as to those wanting to finance large projects that may take years. Besides, the role is not limited to financing. It extends to areas such as insurance and managing foreign-exchange exposure wherever required.  The current global economic and geopolitical uncertainty, which has had a direct impact on international capital flows, indicates that India needs to augment domestic savings to support growth. The BFSI sector clearly has a big role. Further, given India’s development needs, it will nonetheless need foreign capital. Thus, it will be important to quickly address concerns raised in this context by both foreign direct and portfolio investors.   Topics : Business Standard BFSI Summit BFSI Business Standard Editorial Comment Indian Economy Mutual Funds BS Opinion

entry.title: A stunning turnaround
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / A stunning turnaroundA stunning turnaround

Lula da Silva has multiple challenges

premium

Brazil President, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva(Photo:PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:34 PM ISTThe re-election of Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva as President of Brazil has come as a shock to both markets and his domestic Opposition. His challenger, Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of the controversial former President, Jair Bolsonaro, had taken a handy lead in the first round of the presidential elections. This led, perhaps, to a certain degree of overconfidence among the right-wing challengers. In the end, thanks to an enormous effort to increase the turnout, the incumbent President pulled through a second-round victory, which didn’t appear close. This has never happened in Brazil’s history. For Mr Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, this election will no doubt be his last. But it will cement his reputation as South America’s most influential democratic left-wing politician of the past century. His story, from his beginning as a metal-worker, to his time in the trade unions, to victories in presidential elections, will inspire left-wingers across the continent, especially because much of the rest of it is dominated by the right.  President Lula’s last election was marred by what amounted to an abortive coup attempt launched by Jair Bolsonaro’s allies. Fortunately, there appears to be no such effort in progress on this occasion. The challenges for Mr Lula this time will be external. It is not his domestic Opposition but global markets that will revolt. And United States President Donald Trump has made no secret of his sympathy for Mr Bolsonaro, and has already declared that the election to him “looked rigged”. Of these two adversaries, the markets are the more concerning at present. Flavio Bolsonaro, in the course of his campaign, stressed the poor macroeconomic situation that Brazil was in. The numbers are, indeed, worrying. In the four years since Jair Bolsonaro was ousted in 2022, the country’s debt-to-gross domestic product ratio has increased from about 72 per cent to about 83 per cent. High interest costs and the left’s spending commitments make debt servicing quite hard; and there is no credible path towards consolidation that Mr Lula has laid out.  Unsurprisingly, the surprise news that he had been re-elected caused markets to fall. The stock market fell almost 14 per cent in one day, hitting the circuit breaker. Brazil’s currency, the real, fell more than 8 per cent against the dollar, its sharpest one-day drop since 2002. Real-denominated 10-year bond yields rose by more than 2 percentage points, hitting around 15 per cent. All of this deeply complicates Mr Lula’s attempts at stabilisation. He will not want to cut spending or benefits, and indeed plans to increase the wages (and thereby affect the path of future pensions, worsening the fiscal situation). But he cannot raise taxes easily to compensate because his party does not control the legislature, which has repeatedly resisted any attempt to raise the effective tax rate by closing loopholes.  It is likely, therefore, that if Mr Lula wants to work on his legacy over this term, he will look to geopolitics rather than economics. He may well take on the position of primary resister to the new Monroe doctrine that has been espoused by Mr Trump’s second administration. If so, India should expect a Brazil even more committed to counter-mobilisation against the US, and old-style “third-worldism”, than before.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment Brazil Elections Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva

entry.title: Ethanol in the fast lane
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Ethanol in the fast laneEthanol in the fast lane

A slower transition can address unanticipated impacts

premium

The fact that ethanol distilleries tend to be located close to agri-hubs also plays a role in creating employment opportunities and promotes some measure of rural development

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 10:27 PM ISTThe Ministry of Road Transport and Highways’ decision to allow E100 and E85 fuels, along with the registration of flex-fuel vehicles, is understandable in the light of the geopolitical outlook on oil prices in the foreseeable future and growing urban pollution, much of which is transport-related. But the wisdom of such policy speed may need to be balanced with the anticipated negative externalities associated with the ethanol journey. Already, the mandated shift to E20 from E10 five years ahead of the original schedule, prompted no doubt by prolonged supply constraints and the need to meet “Net Zero” targets, has annoyed car owners, who have reported a 7-12 per cent drop in fuel efficiency, which somewhat negates the argument of lowering fuel demand. According to the government data, however, the country has saved ₹1.9 trillion in imports of crude oil and substituted 31 million tonnes between April, when the E20 mandate came into force, and mid-October, though some analysts have questioned the arithmetic behind these calculations.  On the face of it, the drive towards an ethanol-powered automotive future has been a win-win. It has reportedly helped stabilise farm incomes, especially in Bihar, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and Karnataka, by offering a predictable market for agri-surpluses and also absorbing damaged foodgrain from the system. The fact that ethanol distilleries tend to be located close to agri-hubs also plays a role in creating employment opportunities and promotes some measure of rural development. But the long-term impacts on food security and ecology remain open questions. The impact was evident in the sugar market earlier this year, when low opening stocks and production resulted in a sharp rise in sugar prices. Meanwhile, the government has rebutted the accusation of larger diversions of the rice stocks, underlining that Food Corporation of India, the government procurement agency, only diverted damaged or broken grain for ethanol production and did not endanger the food-security programme.  But over time and given the uncertainties of agri-markets, the rapid expansion of the ethanol programme could well incentivise farmers to divert larger tracts of land towards sugar or maize cultivation, which raises a fresh set of problems. This is exemplified by Brazil, which is regarded as a global success story in the ethanol transition. The 25-year transition, which started in 1975, has undoubtedly helped bring about  a sharp reduction in greenhouse-gas emission but has had a deleterious effect on local ecology. As farmers there started converting more and more arable land for maize and sugarcane, they displaced livestock and cattle ranchers, who then simply cleared large tracts of the Amazon rainforest to expand. The country also faced occasional price and supply asymmetries; when global prices of sugar rose, supplies available for the ethanol programme inevitably fell. Equally, the sugar crop was diverted to ethanol producers when ethanol prices rose.  In India, there is also the question of whether promoting water-intensive crops like sugarcane on a large scale for the ethanol programme is warranted when agri-inputs — fertiliser, water, and electricity — are either heavily subsidised or free. On balance, given the complexities of India’s agricultural policies, it may be better to move more gradually on the ethanol transition rather than steer abruptly into the fast lane.     Topics : Ethanol blending Fuel ethanol Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment

Today's editorials and columns examine foreign portfolio outflows, municipal governance, capital-gains taxation, RBI liquidity management and a book exploring the science of brain health

R Kavita Rao, director of the National Institute of Public Finance and Policy, advocates a review of securities transaction tax and a stable capital taxation framework amid foreign investor outflows and rupee depreciation. | Illustration: Binay Sinha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 30 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. 

 

Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have sold more than Rs 2.9 trillion of Indian stocks this year, contributing to the Nifty’s 12 per cent fall, but domestic investors and strong IPO demand have helped sustain the market. India led globally in IPO numbers in 2025, while domestic institutions have bought over Rs 7 trillion in shares this year. With economic growth and corporate results holding up, global risk aversion is driving much of the foreign selling. Today's first editorial recommends that the Indian government review tax policies to improve post-tax dollar returns for foreign investors and consider fairer tax treatment across investments. India’s cities need stronger, more autonomous municipal governments to manage rapid urbanisation and sustain economic growth, the second editorial says. With the urban population projected to reach 850 million by 2050, fragmented responsibilities, weak mayoral powers, delayed elections and inadequate municipal revenues hamper planning and service delivery. Infrastructure spending alone cannot solve these problems. States should devolve responsibilities along with funds, staff and decision-making powers, while cities improve property-tax collection and other own-source revenues. The editorial recommends beginning reforms in million-plus cities, where institutions and capacity are more developed, and extending them to smaller urban centres. India should not cut capital-gains taxes in haste to stem foreign outflows driven largely by global conditions, writes R Kavita Rao. Despite FPI selling, the economy is forecast to grow by more than 7 per cent and Nifty 50 firms have reported strong revenue and profit growth. Rao says policymakers should examine whether securities transaction tax is still justified alongside capital-gains tax, since it taxes trades rather than income. She cautions against crisis-driven concessions that may encourage round-tripping or prove hard to reverse, and calls for a stable, transparent tax framework serving long-term economic priorities. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) should restore banks’ daily cash-reserve requirement to 90 per cent and use a higher overall CRR to absorb durable excess liquidity, says Janak Raj. The current 99 per cent rule has pushed the weighted average call rate above the corridor ceiling, while disrupting banks’ arbitrage in the call-money market and encouraging precautionary reserves and use of the MSF. Raj says durable liquidity measures would keep the operating rate aligned with the repo rate while preserving market activity. Raising the CRR from its record low could also share liquidity-management costs with banks and rebuild a prudential buffer. In her review of Brain Defenders: Harness the Power of Your Immune Cells to Protect Your Brain for Life, Neha Bhatt says David Perlmutter makes the case for preventing brain disorders by addressing underlying inflammation and the role of microglia. The book links brain health to metabolism, diet, sleep, stress and exercise, and presents emerging research in an accessible, if sometimes technical and repetitive, way. Bhatt finds its discussion of supplements and experimental treatments, including hyperbaric oxygen therapy, more provocative, noting the safety and standardisation concerns. Overall, she calls it a thought-provoking guide to evolving neuroscience.A

Today's editorials and columns examine India's financial sector, gender gaps in apprenticeships, UK-EU carbon-border rules, China's economic vulnerabilities and a book exploring Aligarh's history

India's exporters, particularly MSMEs, face growing compliance challenges as the UK and EU implement their Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) regulations. | Illustration : Binay Sinha

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 29 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page. 

 

India’s resilient growth needs a financial sector able to channel savings into investment, finance projects of every scale and expand insurance and pensions, today’s first editorial says. The economy grew 7.8 per cent in the first quarter, prompting the IMF to raise its annual forecast to 7 per cent, while banks’ gross non-performing loan ratio has fallen to 1.8 per cent. With global uncertainty affecting capital flows, the editorial urges the BFSI sector to mobilise domestic savings and calls for prompt action on concerns raised by foreign investors. Women’s growing participation in apprenticeships is not yet translating into equal access to skilled, better-paid work, the second editorial cautions. Women made up 29.5 per cent of NAPS apprentices in 2026-27, but only 6 per cent of electricians and 2.6 per cent of fitters; some technical trades had none. Training alone is insufficient: care burdens, unsafe travel, workplace conditions and limited job access constrain employment and advancement. The editorial calls for tracking completion, placements, wages and progression, alongside childcare, safe transport, affordable accommodation and effective grievance systems, so policy measures job quality as well as entry. Indian exporters need urgent support to meet the UK and EU carbon-border rules taking effect in 2027, writes Amita Batra. Although the UK recognises India’s carbon-credit system, many small and medium-sized firms lack the monitoring, verification and documentation needed to claim offsets; default emissions values could leave them facing higher charges. The EU’s more granular rules will also require detailed supply-chain data. Batra calls for product-code mapping, funding for emissions-accounting systems, training for exporters and alignment between Indian and European carbon-measurement frameworks to protect the market access offered by recent trade agreements. China faces a dangerous convergence of political succession risks, economic slowdown and weakening public finances, warn Navneeraj Sharma and Arvind Subramanian. The Communist Party has centralised power under Xi Jinping, while property woes, ageing and external trade pressures cloud growth. Its fiscal model is also strained: personal income tax has averaged just 1.2 per cent of GDP over the past decade, and taxes excluding social insurance fell from 18.4 per cent of GDP in 2012 to 12.6 per cent in 2025. The authors caution that even a gradual erosion of growth and state capacity could trigger another global shock. Atif Syed’s Aligarh: The City That Outlasted Empires traces the city’s layered history through archival records and overlooked connections. Saurabh Sharma appreciates Syed’s research, particularly his account of Aligarh’s French families and the city’s syncretic past, but finds much of the book a dry chronicle that may deter general readers. The early origin stories and chapters linking the past to places still present in the city offer more engaging moments. Sharma says the valuable discoveries needed a stronger narrative to make them more accessible.

entry.title: Choices between worthy goals pulling in different directions
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Choices between worthy goals pulling in different directionsChoices between worthy goals pulling in different directions

Good policy lies in balancing competing priorities, from affordability and innovation to inclusion and protection, while ensuring growth, accountability and long-term sustainability

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 27 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTGood policy is not so much about a choice between right and wrong as it is between two worthwhile goals pulling in different directions. Health care must be affordable, but innovation needs incentives. Credit should be easier to access, but data and borrowers need protection. Domestic investors can support markets, but global competitiveness still matters. Boards must supervise without micromanaging. Businesses can pursue purpose, but they cannot ignore economic viability. The difficulty begins when both objectives are legitimate. Our first editorial today, “Pricing pain points”, looks at health care price controls. The impulse to make treatment more affordable is understandable, especially in a country where out-of-pocket medical spending remains high. But blunt price intervention can create unintended consequences by weakening incentives for companies to launch new medicines, invest in innovation or supply products sustainably. The challenge is to improve affordability without undermining the economics that make better treatment possible. Access matters, but so does the capacity to keep producing what patients need. The second editorial, “Seamless credit network”, looks at interoperable digital lending. Better sharing of financial information can make credit more accessible, particularly for borrowers who are poorly served by traditional banking. But greater connectivity also raises questions about consent, privacy, data security, responsible lending and competition. Inclusion cannot come at the cost of weaker safeguards. A credit network becomes genuinely useful only when convenience and protection advance together. In “Risk of irrelevance?”, Akash Prakash talks about the tension in Indian equities. Domestic investors have supported the market even as foreign investors have sold heavily. That is a source of strength, but it should not become a reason to dismiss prolonged underperformance or declining international interest. India still needs to remain attractive to global capital. A deeper domestic investor base can reduce dependence on foreign flows, but it cannot substitute for earnings growth, competitive valuations and confidence in India’s long-term economic prospects. Rama Bijapurkar’s column, “Uneasy lies the governance space”, examines the boundary between boards and management. Boards are meant to challenge, oversee and protect shareholder interests, but not to run the company. Management needs enough freedom to operate effectively, but it cannot be allowed to escape scrutiny. Trouble begins when oversight turns into interference or autonomy turns into unaccountability. Good governance depends on keeping that boundary clear. M S Sriram’s review of Eric Ries’ Incorruptible, “The double-edged sword of a dual bottom line”, confronts the tension between profit and purpose. Organisations that pursue both commercial returns and social objectives can create powerful models, but they also face competing incentives and difficult accountability questions. The hardest systems, these pieces show, are not those with one goal. They are those with two good ones. Success depends on knowing where the balance lies.

entry.title: Pricing pain points

Home / Opinion / Editorial / Pricing pain pointsPricing pain points

Controls in health care are needed but come with risks

premium

The government has acknowledged steep hospital markups on medicines and medical consumables, raising concerns over healthcare affordability and the need for stronger pricing regulations. (Photo: Shutterstock)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 10:10 PM ISTThe government’s admission before the Supreme Court that hospitals routinely overcharge customers for drugs and other products offers a faint hope for a healthier drug-price control regime. But establishing a comprehensive one could be tricky. Western countries that impose limits on drug-pricing margins and manufacturers’ costs — such as Canada or nations of the European Union — do so via near-universal health care programmes that involve bulk (and in that sense monopoly) purchases. India’s health system, on the other hand, is increasingly driven by private-sector delivery, where monitoring price caps is a challenging proposition and largely depends on forbearance on the part of hospitals, clinics and chemists. Nevertheless, the problem is serious enough for the government to consider some level of intervention following the public-interest litigation (PIL), seeking the apex court’s intervention to regulate the prices of generic medicines, drugs and medical equipment. The affidavit had stated that hospital markups on many drugs range between 170 per cent and 700 per cent,  while those on consumables range from 100 per cent to 1,000 per cent. The court itself had described as “dacoity” the markup on the maximum retail price of a range of life-saving drugs, especially cancer drugs. The government has acknowledged that the information asymmetry between patient and hospital is the chief reason for this blatant price gouging. At least part of the problem lies in the government’s drug price-control regime. Medicines are divided into “scheduled” drugs, which are essential medicines that have ceiling prices set by the government — such as insulin, some antibiotics and anti-depressants, tuberculosis medications — and “non-scheduled” drugs, which allow manufacturers to set prices. Over 80 per cent of drugs fall in the non-scheduled category — and that includes cancer drugs. Facing up to this incontrovertible evidence of these pricing practices — that can often tip families into bankruptcy — the government machinery has moved to address the issue. With effect from November 9, 2026, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) has capped the trade margins on 137 anti-cancer drugs at 30 per cent of the maximum retail price (MRP). The intervention is expected to lower the MRP on life-saving cancer drugs by up to 70 per cent. A parliamentary standing committee has recommended — not for the first time — standardising private-hospital costs, capping room rents to three-star hotel rates, and enforcing mandatory disclosure of upfront costs of medical procedures.  The obvious question is the efficacy with which such diktats can be imposed. Drug-price control runs the risk of being self-defeating. The supply of key molecules for several bulk drugs shifted to China after price controls made them unprofitable for local manufacturers. Today, India imports two-thirds of its active pharmaceutical ingredients from China, the impact of which was keenly felt during the Covid lockdown. Countries with price-control regimes have also felt the impact of manufacturers’ reluctance to introduce the latest drugs into those markets. The government, therefore, needs to navigate between producer and retail profiteering and patients’ interests. Widely disseminated education and a multilingual campaign on patient rights and price policies would go a long way in bridging the information gap. The fact that the NPPA falls under the Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilisers rather than the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, which is responsible for health care delivery, suggests a fundamental policy disconnect, which too should be addressed.   Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment BS Opinion high drug prices cancer treatment health care sector Medicine prices

entry.title: Seamless credit network
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Seamless credit networkSeamless credit network

Interoperability can enable inclusive lending

premium

The RBI's push for interoperability among account aggregators aims to simplify consent-based financial data sharing, improve credit access and reduce loan application dropouts.| Photo: Shutterstock

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 26 2026 | 10:08 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) decision to introduce interoperability among account aggregators (AAs) by December 31 seeks to simplify financial-data sharing, which could help reduce loan-application dropoffs. The need for this is underlined by the rapid growth of the AA ecosystem. According to the CRIF Credit Information Services and industry alliance Sahamati, the AA framework facilitated an estimated ₹3.82 trillion in loan disbursements across 36.8 million accounts in 2025-26, accounting for 8.4 per cent of retail lending and loans to micro, small and medium enterprises by value and 11.8 per cent by volume. By September, the ecosystem had fulfilled 595 million consents. More importantly, it is reaching borrowers often overlooked by conventional lending models. In the year ended June 2026, borrowers new to credit accounted for 28.5 per cent of business loans worth ₹10 lakh-25 lakh issued by AA-enabled lenders, against 8.6 per cent for other lenders. In personal loans, their share was 9 per cent, compared with 3.8 per cent through conventional channels. In 2025-26, the value of AA-enabled lending was estimated to be about 1.1 per cent of India’s gross domestic product.  The framework addresses a longstanding problem in the Indian lending ecosystem. Individuals and small businesses without established credit histories often struggle to obtain formal loans even when they have regular incomes or viable businesses. Traditional assessments rely heavily on credit history and require borrowers to submit bank statements, tax documents, and other paperwork. The AA framework allows lenders to access financial information directly from participating institutions, with borrowers’ consent. This enables a more comprehensive assessment of repayment capacity. Its benefits extend beyond loan approvals. The study found that, in lending for two-wheelers, the share of loans overdue by more than 90 days was 0.5 per cent for AA-enabled originations, compared with 5.3 per cent for conventional loans. Greater access, therefore, need not come at the cost of weaker credit quality.  However, differences in technical standards, system reliability, and integration costs could undermine the benefits. Banks, non-banking financial companies, and AA platforms must adopt common protocols, ensure reliable data transfers, and minimise transaction failures. Transparent pricing and clear accountability for failed consent requests or incomplete data sharing will also be necessary. Data protection is equally important. Financial information can reveal sensitive details about an individual’s income, spending and liabilities. Strong encryption, access controls, independent security audits, and effective grievance redress are essential to maintain public trust. It is also important to ensure that smaller lenders are not disadvantaged by high integration costs. Research by the RBI-promoted Centre for Advanced Financial Research and Learning has associated greater exposure to the AA rollout with higher local economic activity. While this does not establish that AAs alone caused the increase, it points to their wider potential. Interoperability can help realise that potential provided efficiency is matched by safeguards. Better data sharing should make credit easier to access without compromising borrowers’ privacy or financial security. With 17 AAs operating in the ecosystem, better connectivity with banks, insurers and pension-related institutions could enable consent-based sharing of a broader range of financial information for inclusion.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Bank credit RBI lending loans Loan pricing
